\chapter*{Pronunciation --- a reference, not a chapter}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{Pronunciation (reference)}
\markboth{Pronunciation}{Pronunciation}

This is a \textbf{reference}, not a chapter. You are not meant to read it front to back before starting. Each lesson tells you the one or two sounds you need for \emph{that} word, and links here if you want the fuller picture. Look things up as curiosity strikes; otherwise, keep learning words.

Each entry has an id (e.g. \texttt{silent-h}) that lessons cite in their frontmatter \texttt{sounds:} field, so \textquotedblleft{}Sounds you'll need\textquotedblright{} notes and this page stay in sync.

\section*{Vowels — the five pure sounds}

Spanish has exactly five vowel sounds, one per letter, every time. English has a dozen-plus and reuses letters for several; that habit is the thing to unlearn.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item \texttt{vowel-a} — \textbf{a} as in English \emph{father}. Always. Never \emph{cat}, never \emph{cake}.
  \item \texttt{vowel-e} — \textbf{e} as in \emph{bed}. Always. Never the \emph{ee} of \emph{see}.
  \item \texttt{vowel-i} — \textbf{i} as the \emph{ee} in \emph{see} (not the English \emph{i} of \emph{sit}). The single most common vowel mistake English speakers make.
  \item \texttt{vowel-o} — \textbf{o} as in \emph{note}, but short and clean, with no \emph{w}-glide at the end.
  \item \texttt{vowel-u} — \textbf{u} as the \emph{oo} in \emph{food}. Always.
\end{itemize}

\section*{Diphthongs — two vowels run together}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item \texttt{diphthong-ue} — \textbf{ue} as a quick \emph{weh} (Spanish \emph{u} + \emph{e}), e.g. \emph{bueno}, \emph{nueve}.
  \item \texttt{diphthong-ie} — \textbf{ie} as a quick \emph{yeh} (Spanish \emph{i} + \emph{e}), e.g. \emph{quiero}, \emph{siete}.
  \item \texttt{diphthong-ei} — \textbf{ei} as in English \emph{they}, e.g. \emph{seis}, \emph{treinta}.
\end{itemize}

\section*{Consonants that differ from English}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item \texttt{silent-h} — \textbf{h} is always silent, no exceptions. \emph{hola} is \emph{OH-la}, \emph{hay} is \emph{eye}.
  \item \texttt{soft-c} — \textbf{c} before \emph{e} or \emph{i} is a soft sound: \emph{s} in Latin America, a \emph{th} (as in \emph{think}) in most of Spain. \emph{gracias}, \emph{cero}. Before \emph{a/o/u} it's a hard \emph{k} (\emph{casa}).
  \item \texttt{qu-k} — \textbf{qu} is a hard \emph{k}, and the \textbf{u is silent}: \emph{quiero} is \emph{KYEH-ro}, \emph{qué} is \emph{keh}. (This silent-\emph{u}-after-\emph{q} is inherited straight from Latin.)
  \item \texttt{ll-y} — \textbf{ll} sounds like English \emph{y} in \emph{yes} across most of Latin America: \emph{llamo} is \emph{YA-mo}. (Regional variation exists; \emph{y} is the safe default.)
  \item \texttt{n-tilde} — \textbf{ñ} is the \emph{ny} of \emph{canyon}: \emph{español} is \emph{es-pa-NYOL}. A different letter from \emph{n}, not a decoration.
  \item \texttt{rr-trill} — \textbf{rr} is a rolled/trilled \emph{r}; a single \emph{r} between vowels is a light tap. \emph{pero} (but) vs. \emph{perro} (dog) is a real minimal pair.
  \item \texttt{j-h} — \textbf{j} is a throat-\emph{h}, rougher than English \emph{h} (like the \emph{ch} in Scottish \emph{loch}): \emph{jueves}.
  \item \texttt{g-soft} — \textbf{g} before \emph{e/i} is the same throat sound as \emph{j} (\emph{gente}); before \emph{a/o/u} it's a hard \emph{g} (\emph{gato}).
  \item \texttt{d-soft} — \textbf{d} between vowels softens toward English \emph{th} in \emph{this}: \emph{nada} is closer to \emph{NA-tha}.
  \item \texttt{v-b} — \textbf{v} and \textbf{b} sound essentially identical in Spanish, both a soft \emph{b}.
\end{itemize}

\section*{Stress \& written accents}

Three facts cover almost every word:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item \texttt{stress-default-vowel-ns} — a word ending in a vowel, \emph{n}, or \emph{s} is stressed on the \textbf{second-to-last} syllable: \emph{ca-SA}, \emph{ha-BLAN}, \emph{li-BROS}.
  \item \texttt{stress-default-consonant} — a word ending in any other consonant is stressed on the \textbf{last} syllable: \emph{ha-BLAR}, \emph{ciu-DAD}.
  \item \texttt{accent-mark} — a written accent (´) overrides both rules and puts the stress exactly on the marked vowel: \emph{ha-BLÓ}, \emph{DÍ-as}. The mark can also distinguish otherwise-identical words (\emph{qué} \textquotedblleft{}what?\textquotedblright{} vs. \emph{que} \textquotedblleft{}that\textquotedblright{}, \emph{tú} \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} vs. \emph{tu} \textquotedblleft{}your\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \texttt{accent-i} — a specific case of the above: the accent on \emph{í} in words like \emph{días} keeps the stress on the \emph{i} where the default rule would otherwise misplace it.
\end{itemize}

\section*{Punctuation}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item \texttt{inverted-marks} — questions and exclamations open with an inverted mark: \emph{¿cómo estás?}, \emph{¡hola!} — so you know the intonation before you reach the end of the sentence.
\end{itemize}
